messages.subject: Comparability of results btw. ANOVA & SEM
messages.subject_clean: Comparability of results btw. ANOVA & SEM
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,
me and my colleagues are new to the SEM world and are struggling to reconcile the ANOVA and SEM results. We hope, you can help us explaining what is going on in our analysis by answering a couple of our questions. (I am sorry right away if I do not use the terminology correctly).

###########################################################
Let me give you some background. We are trying to predict a binomial endogenous variable  (our dependent variable) by means of a set of categorical exogenous variables (our predictors) that all have two levels. But I'd like to focus only on one of those combinations.
Our levels are basically zeros and ones. The table below shows you the distribution of our data:

     endo
exo    0   1
 0 993   9
 1 960  99

The typical approach in my community would be to fit a glm, that transforms the data into logits. When I fit a glm with this data in the for like this:
mod <- glm(pre~br)

I get the following results:

         Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
(Intercept)  -4.0662     0.3361 -12.098  < 2e-16 ***
endo = 1            1.1555     0.4105   2.815  0.00487 **

informing me that the difference between 0 and 1 is logit = 1.155.

We found that when one uses binomial variables, SEM can be informed about this by setting "ordered = TRUE".  When I run the following model:

mod1 <-lavaan::sem('pre ~ br', data=DF, ordered = TRUE)

I get the following summary:

Regressions:
                  Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
  endo ~
   exo                1.047    0.134    7.809    0.000

telling me that the effect of the exogenous variable is significant. However, what does the estimate mean? What does the estimate represent? How is this value calculated and why does it differ from the glm?

#################################################
Another question that arose is that when I fit another relation, I get the following warning message:

  The variance-covariance matrix of the estimated paramet
ers (vcov)
   does not appear to be positive definite! The smallest e
igenvalue
   (= 5.421011e-20) is close to zero. This may be a sympto
m that the
   model is not identified.

I understand that the model failed to converge, but I wonder why, given that the glm fitted the data without problems:

Coefficients:
           Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
(Intercept)   -20.57     819.59  -0.025    0.980
endo = 1             18.53     819.59   0.023    0.982

The failure to converge is even more surprising given that when I set "ordered = FALSE", it runs smoothly and provides me with a result.

################################################################

Another aspect concerns level of significance.
When I fit the exogenous only with one endogenous variable, then SEM informs me that there is no significant effect. However, when I include multiple endogenous variables, it turns out to be significant. Is this because SEMs suffer from something like collinearity that may cause enhancement?

Thank you very much for your help.

messages.subject: Phi matrix vs. Psi matrix
messages.subject_clean: Phi matrix vs. Psi matrix
messages.body_plain:
When I run  lavInspect on the   HolzingerSwineford1939  (or any other )  dataset, it shows the LV correlations under the psi matrix, like this:

$psi
        visual textul speed
visual  1.000
textual 0.459  1.000
speed   0.471  0.283  1.000

Aren't these LV correlations supposed to be called the "phi" matrix and not the "psi" matrix? My understanding of the terminology (e.g., Bollen 1989) is that phi is for the covariances of the exogenous LV (here: visual, textual, speed), and psi is for the covariances of the disturbance terms for endogenous LVs (none here).

Here is the code I used:
HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '
fit <- cfa(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939)
lavInspect(fit, what="std.all", add.labels=T)

messages.subject: Re: Phi matrix vs. Psi matrix
messages.subject_clean: Phi matrix vs. Psi matrix
messages.body_plain:
Back in 1989--more than 30 years ago now--the dominant framework was probably the old LISREL framework, which made distinctions between "the X side": and "the Y side" of the model. When computers were slower and computer time more precious, this may have produced some economies (because it made for smaller parameter matrices) and may have been "more familiar" to researchers with backgrounds in regression. More recently, more researchers have dropped the "X / Y" distinction. If the "Psi" matrix is the matrix of unexplained or unpredicted covariance among common factors, well, these factors have no predictors, so all of their variance is unexplained. But if you like, you can also think of this as a partitioned matrix:

"Psi" =  Phi    0
              0     Psi

Even after all this time, I don't think that anyone has written a better book about factor-based SEM than Bollen (1989).

messages.subject: Re: Phi matrix vs. Psi matrix
messages.subject_clean: Phi matrix vs. Psi matrix
messages.body_plain:
lavaan uses the so-called 'LISREL all-y' notation by default. This
corresponds to LISREL submodel 3B. In this all-y model, all observed
variables ('x' or 'y') are collected in the y-vector, and all latent
variables are collected in the 'eta' vector. Despite being a 'submodel',
it is in fact (a bit) more general than the original LISREL model (as we
can for examample correlate the residual variances of 'x' and 'y'
variables).

According to the 'official' notation of LISREL submodel 3B, the
variance/covariance matrix of the latent variables is denoted by 'Psi'.
It contains both total (for exogenous) and residual (for endogenous)
variances and covariances of 'eta'.

Alternative notations are the 'Bentler-Weeks' notation, and the (many
variants of the) 'Recticular Action Meta-model' (RAM) representation.

In recent versions of lavaan, you can use the representation = "RAM"
argument to switch to a RAM representation, while the default is
representation = "LISREL".

Yves.

You did not supply the data, which should be the raw data given that you use FIML. I can reproduce your error using the example in the help page of cfa().

Add "data =" and specify the data frame. E.g. suppose the raw data is in a data frame rawdata:

allgroups <- cfa(model, data = rawdata, missing = "FIML", fixed.x=FALSE,  meanstructure= TRUE)

Omitting "data =" is also OK as it is the second argument:

allgroups <- cfa(model, rawdata, missing = "FIML", fixed.x=FALSE,  meanstructure= TRUE)

Hope this helps.

-- Shu Fai

messages.body_plain:
Finding the estimates in a model with both ordinal variables and missing data handled by FIML sometimes can be quite difficult, and more so if the number of variables is large. It may take very long to find the solution, and sometimes it may just fail. The issue may be more a model+data one rather than a lavaan one.

"lavaan 0.6-11 ended normally after X iterations"

Hello all –

I'm also on Fabian's team for this project, and we'd be appreciative of any help in figuring out why we see this discrepancy in our results! On Friday, 1 July 2022 at 09:53:35 UTC+1 fabian.t...@googlemail.com wrote:
> Dear All,
> me and my colleagues are new to the SEM world and are struggling to reconcile the ANOVA and SEM results. We hope, you can help us explaining what is going on in our analysis by answering a couple of our questions. (I am sorry right away if I do not use the terminology correctly).
>
> ###########################################################
> Let me give you some background. We are trying to predict a binomial endogenous variable  (our dependent variable) by means of a set of categorical exogenous variables (our predictors) that all have two levels. But I'd like to focus only on one of those combinations.
> Our levels are basically zeros and ones. The table below shows you the distribution of our data:
>
>      endo
> exo    0   1
>  0 993   9
>  1 960  99
>
> The typical approach in my community would be to fit a glm, that transforms the data into logits. When I fit a glm with this data in the for like this:
> mod <- glm(pre~br)
>
> I get the following results:
>
>
>          Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
> (Intercept)  -4.0662     0.3361 -12.098  < 2e-16 ***
> endo = 1            1.1555     0.4105   2.815  0.00487 **
>
>
> informing me that the difference between 0 and 1 is logit = 1.155.
>
> We found that when one uses binomial variables, SEM can be informed about this by setting "ordered = TRUE".  When I run the following model:
>
> mod1 <-lavaan::sem('pre ~ br', data=DF, ordered = TRUE)
>
> I get the following summary:
>
> Regressions:
>                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
>   endo ~
>    exo                1.047    0.134    7.809    0.000
>
>
> telling me that the effect of the exogenous variable is significant. However, what does the estimate mean? What does the estimate represent? How is this value calculated and why does it differ from the glm?
>
>
> #################################################
> Another question that arose is that when I fit another relation, I get the following warning message:
>
>   The variance-covariance matrix of the estimated paramet
> ers (vcov)
>    does not appear to be positive definite! The smallest e
> igenvalue
>    (= 5.421011e-20) is close to zero. This may be a sympto
> m that the
>    model is not identified.
>
> I understand that the model failed to converge, but I wonder why, given that the glm fitted the data without problems:
>
> Coefficients:
>            Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
> (Intercept)   -20.57     819.59  -0.025    0.980
> endo = 1             18.53     819.59   0.023    0.982
>
> The failure to converge is even more surprising given that when I set "ordered = FALSE", it runs smoothly and provides me with a result.
>
>
> ################################################################
>
> Another aspect concerns level of significance.
> When I fit the exogenous only with one endogenous variable, then SEM informs me that there is no significant effect. However, when I include multiple endogenous variables, it turns out to be significant. Is this because SEMs suffer from something like collinearity that may cause enhancement?
>
> Thank you very much for your help.
>
>
>

I just want to share with you Dr. Rosseel's response here.

The errors like what I posted above will come out with a small dataset with ordered variables.
You can fix the bug in the sam()function by setting se ="none"; however, you can get only partial results.

In my case, my sample size is 346. With se ="none",  I was only able to get estimate results.
Thank you so much for your response, Dr. Rosseel again :)

------ follow-up question
I have follow-up questions to continue to make factor score path analyses work.

It seems like Croon's correction with ordinal variables is not available with sufficient results yet.
Also, I found it hard to use Croon's correction for factor score path analyses when the measurement models are a bit complex - for example, bi-factor model or models with corss-loading indicators, etc. I also tried to treat my ordinal variables as continuous (since it is 4-6 Likert scale) to use sam()function, but the model fit was horrible because of (I assumed) cross-loading indicators and unused factors in the model.

All factor score determinacies of my variables (which are coded as ordinal) are > .80, so it is pretty good.
In this case, would it be okay to use the factor scores extracted from lavaan for path analyses without factor score correction?
Or is there any other simple way to correct factor scores (although it may not as effective as Croon's) to take factor score uncertainty into account?

Thank you so much in advance.

Sincerely,
Jun

Fawad,

The "cluster" argument in lavaan() is, as far as I know, equivalent to the "complex" statement in Mplus. In both cases, it estimate relations among level-1 variables, adjusting for clustering.

If you are interested in relations among level-2 (between) variables, I'm pretty sure lavaan doesn't do that yet.

Pat

messages.subject_clean: Comparability of results btw. ANOVA & SEM
messages.body_plain:
Please provide a minimal reproducible example for assistance with errors and discrepancies (see  https://stackoverflow.com/help/minimal-reproducible-example)

It appears that "ordered" models the endogenous variables with the probit link based on the cumulative normal rather than the logit based on the cumulative logistic. These may differ at times, although usually modestly. Numerical error also can produce slightly different results if tolerances, starting values, etc. differ. See https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/mG5Mjrf2jgo/m/YGC-kR9oDAAJ

If you need help understanding SEM more generally - interpretation, covariance structures, assumptions, dealing with non-normality, etc. - I'd recommend picking up a SEM text like Bollen (1989) and eventually visiting the SEMNet archives. If you want to know in more detail what the black box of the software is doing, you'll want to review this group and read the lavaan paper(s).

Hello there,

I am analyzing a dataset that utilizing time sampling to predict loneliness. I am struggling to add control variables at level 1 in order to see how age may predict momentary affect in addition to person-level affect. All variable on level 1 are time-varying, while those on level 2 are person-level variables.

modelwithage<- '
level : 1
  SA_Last ~ a1*NA_First
  SIDay2 ~ a2*SA_Last
  LNDay3 ~ a3*SIDay2
  LNDay3 ~ c_1*NA_First
  indirect1 := a1*a2*a3
  total1 := c_1 + indirect1
Level : 2
  SA_Last_mean ~ a_1*NA_First_mean + age
  SI_Day2_mean ~ a_2*SA_Last_mean  + age
  LNDay3_mean ~ a_3*SI_Day2_mean  + age
  LNDay3_mean ~ c_2*NA_First_mean
  indirect2 := a_1*a_2*a_3

'

How then do I control for age at this level?

Thank you!

Meagan

messages.subject: Re: Interpretation of coeffiecients between binary exogenous and endogenous variables estimated with WLSMV
messages.subject_clean: Interpretation of coeffiecients between binary exogenous and endogenous variables estimated with WLSMV
messages.body_plain:
In robust WLS estimation (e.g., WLSMV), and focusing on the standardized solution, the beta coefficients estimate the amount of standard deviation change in the latent response variable (LRV) for each one standard deviation  increase  in the predictor. This interpretation is the same whether you applied delta or theta parameterization.
If you want to focus on the unstandardized solution:
Delta parameterization (total variance of LRV fixed to 1): coefficients estimate the amount of unit change in the LRV for each one unit  increase  in the predictor.
Theta parameterization (residual variance of LRV fixed to 1):  coefficients estimate the amount of change in probit (normal deviate) units in the LRV for each one unit increase in the predictor.
Source: Kline (2016, Ch. 13)

Hi!

I am stuck on trying to find the p-value for mean.lv <http://mean.lv> on a multigroup SEM.
This is my first interaction with the group, so sorry if I made something wrong. I tried to find discussions about this topic, but the closest one I found apparently do not faced the same problem (and was about CFA)

My apologies if it is duplicated.
And thank you very much!!!

The problem: Evaluating the mean.lv <http://mean.lv> estimation on a Multigroup SEM:

model <-'
A = x1+x2+x3
B = x4+x5+x6

messages.subject: Re: Latent Means PValue - Multi Group SEM
messages.subject_clean: Latent Means PValue - Multi Group SEM
messages.body_plain:
When a variable is exogneous, it doesn't have a mean, it only has an intercept. The expected value depends on the value of the predictors - for the intercept it says "This is the expected value if the predictors all have the value zero", but you can choose any value - zero is arbitrary, and the value you pick will change the expected value.

Because the groups have different means for C and D, you might want to evaluate the differences at the mean of C and D, or you might want to evaluate the differences when they are equal. It also depends on whether the regression slopes are equal.  If the slopes aren't equal (and I forget the default - I like to specify everything in the mode, and not rely on defaults) then it's a bit of a weird comparison (probably).

I hope that makes sense,

Jeremy

messages.subject: Re: new to R
messages.subject_clean: new to R
messages.body_plain:
R all the way. :)

One advantage of using R all the way is that you can have one workflow, you read in your data, clean / manipulate, and analyze in one script.  That way you have one script that you can run that will do your analysis - you don't lose track of which prep script goes with which Amos file. You can even write the whole paper using RMarkdown - if you find an error in the raw data, you just fix it and then hit run and your paper is rewritten.

It's a bit of a hump to get over - you will spend a little while being frustrated, and using your favorite search engine to find how to do things, but once you have got over that hump the advantages  easily outweigh the disadvantages  (IMHO).

 I don't have access to (or need) SPSS (or SAS, or Stata ...).

J

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I´m sure this must be a simple question, but as this is my first work on LGM and I could not find any information on this, I hope you can help me.

I am doing a linear LGM with 4 time points and group as time-invariant variable. So far I have learned that it should look like this when I have two groups:

model_growth <- '

i =~ 1*time1 + 1*time2 + 1*time3 + 1*time4
s =~ 0*time1+ 1*time2 + 2*time3 + 3*time4

i + s ~ groups

  '
fit_growth <- growth(model_growth, data=wide_dat, missing = "fiml")
summary(fit_growth, fit.measures=TRUE, standardized=TRUE, rsquare=TRUE)

Then I can interpret the the difference in the slope as the difference between group one and two and look at the significance. But is it also possible to compare latent intercepts and slopes for 4 groups at once? If I code it like this: "i + s ~ groups" with four groups it doesn´t look like it makes any sense. I would like to analyse differences between all 4, for ex. group 1 compared to 2, group one compared to 3,4 and so on.

Do I have to make different models for each pair of group to compare all of them or is there an easier way? If so, can someone give me a coding and interpretation example?

I would be grateful for any help! Thank you in advance!

Best regards,
Deni

messages.subject: RE: reference group in multiple group CFA
messages.subject_clean: reference group in multiple group CFA
messages.body_plain:
Hi Frank,

Let's start with a simple 3 group model and simulate some data:

library(lavaan)

pop.model <- "f =~ 1.0 * x1 + 0.9 * x2 + 0.9 * x3"

n = 10000

set.seed(1)

data <- rbind(

  simulateData(paste(pop.model, "f ~ 1.0 * 1", sep = "\n"), sample.nobs = n),

  simulateData(paste(pop.model, "f ~ 2.0 * 1", sep = "\n"), sample.nobs = n),

  simulateData(paste(pop.model, "f ~ 2.4 * 1", sep = "\n"), sample.nobs = n)

)

data$g <- rep(1 : 3, each = n)

The mean of the lv in the first group is 1.0, the mean of the lv in the second group is 2.0, and the mean of the lv in the third group is 2.4. We specify the model and set an arbitrary mean value for the lv in any group. This group is now the "reference group". We specify the mean differences using parameters:

model <- "

f =~ x1 + x2 + x3

f ~ c(m1, m2, m3)

m1 == 10

diff.g2.g1 := m2 - m1

diff.g3.g1 := m3 - m1

diff.g3.g2 := m3 - m2

"

In our case, the mean value of the lv in the first group is 10. The first group is thus the "reference group". We fit the model and obtain the correct mean differences:

fit <- cfa(model, data, group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts"), meanstructure = TRUE, group = "g")

pe  <- parameterestimates(fit)

pe[pe$op == ":=",]

Since we can also set the mean of the "reference group" to zero (which is common), two out of three mean differences are provided "free of charge":

model <- "

f =~ x1 + x2 + x3

f ~ c(m1, m2, m3) * 1

m1 == 0

diff.g2.g1 := m2 - m1

diff.g3.g1 := m3 - m1

diff.g3.g2 := m3 - m2

"

fit <- cfa(model, data, group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts"), meanstructure = TRUE, group = "g")

pe  <- parameterestimates(fit)

pe[pe$op == "~1" & pe$lhs == "f",]

pe[pe$op == ":=",]

One could come up with the idea to completely abandon the definition of a "reference group" by applying effect coding:

model <- "

f =~ x1 + x2 + x3

f ~ c(m1, m2, m3) * 1

diff.g2.g1 := m2 - m1

diff.g3.g1 := m3 - m1

diff.g3.g2 := m3 - m2

"

fit <- cfa(model, data, effect.coding = TRUE, group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts"), meanstructure = TRUE, group = "g")

pe  <- parameterestimates(fit)

pe[pe$op == ":=",]

Note: The results are obviously biased (which was to be expected)!

HTH

Christian

messages.body_plain:
The impact of reverse coding should be to reverse the signs of observed variable correlations. If sample size is low and model fit is somewhat marginal, it is possible that flipping the signs of correlations could produce an ill-conditioned correlation matrix. But there may also be an interaction with the specific algorithm that lavaan uses to optimize fit. This kind of pattern may not have been tested as heavily during software development.
Try setting starting values for the parameter estimates related to the reverse coded item. You might choose as starting values the parameter estimates from the model that converged but with reversed signs. You might also try a maximum likelihood solution, just to see if the behavior is specific to WLSMV.

Scalar invariance implies metric invariance, so if full metric invariance fails then full scalar invariance has already failed.

messages.subject: Multi-group comparison for RI-CLPM
messages.subject_clean: Multi-group comparison for RI-CLPM
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am hoping someone can help with a question I have.  I’m running a RI-CLPM in which two variables were assessed at 5 occasions over time in each of two distinct groups of subjects and we want to see if the model parameters differ across groups.  It’s pretty straightforward to set up a multi-group comparison to test whether the groups differ in the magnitudes of the cross-lagged paths.  However, we also would also like to see if the groups differ in their random intercepts for each variable (mean levels of each variable over time).  Typically, I would just include Group as a predictor of each random intercept, but I’d prefer to test both forms of moderation (values of the random intercept and magnitudes of the cross-paths) in the same model.  I assume there is a straightforward way to accomplish this that I am just missing.  Any help would be greatly appreciated.

Thanks,
Brandon

Professor
Director, Mood Disorders Institute <http://mood.binghamton.edu/>
Department of Psychology
Binghamton University (SUNY)
Binghamton, NY

messages.subject_clean: ML method or Least square method
messages.body_plain:
This is not directly related to the estimation of the coefficients. Non-normally distributed data are problematic for inferential statistical tests, since se and chi-squared can be biased. There are more or less good solutions for this, such as robust ML estimators or bootstrapping. More or less, because even these methods are not free of assumptions.

Best

Christian

messages.subject_clean: ML method or Least square method
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mona,

As Christian mentioned, Robust Maximum Likelihood deals pretty well with non-normality. You can change this in your CFA syntax by adding the argument "estimator = MLR". If you are looking for resources to back this up and /or learn more about it, please check the following:

Zhong, X., & Yuan, K. H. (2011). Bias and efficiency in structural equation modeling: Maximum likelihood versus robust methods. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 46(2), 229-265.

Using MLR also helps to alleviate concerns of bias on the fit indices (e.g., RMSEA, CFI). This is the resource for this:

Brosseau-Liard, P. E., Savalei, V., & Li, L. (2012). An investigation of the sample performance of two nonnormality corrections for RMSEA. Multivariate behavioral research, 47(6), 904-930.

You might also want to check a previous post in this group with answers from Prof. Rosseel and Prof. Jorgensen:

https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/9umZmFsvX3M

Hope this helps.

Alejandro

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone, I am having some troubles in defing the correct code for calculating the sample size for a new model that I built. I attached the hypothesized model. I have a few questions: Is it the code that I am using the correct one for my aim? 2. Should I include the residual variances and covariances? If yes, how can I set them since I don't have any references for it? I used the studies that I cited to support my hypotheses to set both factor loadings and coefficients, but I don't have any info about the residual covariances and variances. Should I set them according to standard value? Thank you very much for your help!

Here above the syntax that I was thinking to use:

#I set the  factor loadings according to literature

popModel <- "
#measurament model
sti =~ 0.49*s1 + 0.72*s2 + 0.88*s3
su =~ 0.6*su1 + 0.6*su2 + 0.6*su3
pc =~ 0.85*p1 + 0.87*p2 + 0.79*p3
ic =~ 0.65*i1 + 0.63*i2 + 0.83*i3
att =~ 0.84*a1 + 0.86*a2 + 0.86*a3
sn =~ 0.87*sn1 + 0.91*sn2 + 0.89*sn3
pbc =~ 0.83*pb1 + 0.92*pb2 + 0.80*pb3 + 0.85*pb4
int =~ 0.90*in1 + 0.90*in2 + 0.91*in3
pb =~ 1*pb1

#structural model

att ~ -0.67*sti + 0.19*su + 0.25*pc + 0.25*ic
sn ~ 0.20*su
pbc ~ 0.19*su
int ~ 0.30*att + 0.28*sn + 0.37*pbc + 0.18*pb

"
analysis.mod  <- '
# define latent variables
sti =~ s1 + s2 + s3
su =~ su1 + su2 + su3
pc =~ p1 + p2 + p3
ic =~ i1 + i2 + i3
att =~ a1 + a2 + a3
sn =~ sn1 + sn2 + sn3
pbc =~ pb1 + pb2 + pb3 + pb4
int =~ in1 + in2 + in3
pb =~ pb1

# specify structural model

att ~ b8*sti + b1*su + b10*pc + b11*ic
sn ~ b3*su
pbc ~ b5*su
int ~ b2*att + b4*sn + b6*pbc + b7*pb + b12*su

# indirect effects
su.att.int <http://su.att.int> := b1*b2
su.sn.int <http://su.sn.int> := b3*b4
su.pbc.int <http://su.pbc.int> := b5*b6

# total effects

att.int <http://att.int> := b12 + b1*b2
sn.int <http://sn.int> := b12 +b3*b4
pbc.int <http://pbc.int> := b12 + b5*b6'

# A) run simulation (varying sample sizes)
med.n <- simsem::sim(n=rep(seq(100,500,20),100), # varying sample sizes (each 100x)
                     model=analysis.mod,
                     generate=pop.mod,
                     lavaanfun="sem")

summary(med.n)
med.n <- sim(5, n=100, model = analysis.mod, generate =  pop.mod, lavaanfun = "sem", seed=1234)

?seq
# B) The varying parameter value that provides the power just over the specified power value
# (the adjacent value of varying parameter provides lower power than the specified power value).
powTable2 <- getPower(med.n)
findPower(powTable2, "N", 0.85)

# su.att.int <http://su.att.int> --> N1
# su.sn.int <http://su.sn.int>  --> N2
# su.pbc.int <http://su.pbc.int>  --> N3

# C) power curves
plotPower(med.n, powerParam = "su.att.int <http://su.att.int>")
abline(h = 0.85, lwd = 2, lty = 2)

plotPower(med.n, powerParam = "su.sn.int <http://su.sn.int> ")
abline(h = 0.85, lwd = 2, lty = 2)

plotPower(med.n, powerParam = "su.pbc.int <http://su.pbc.int>")
abline(h = 0.85, lwd = 2, lty = 2)

# D) 2 simulations with n=264 (10.000 repetitions) with two different seeds
med.n.neu1 <- simsem::sim(nRep=10000, model=analysis.mod, n=264, generate=pop.mod, lavaanfun="sem", seed=9999)
med.n.neu2 <- simsem::sim(nRep=10000, model=analysis.mod, n=264, generate=pop.mod, lavaanfun="sem", seed=99)

round(summaryParam(med.n.neu1, alpha=0.05, detail=TRUE), digits=3)
round(summaryParam(med.n.neu2, alpha=0.05), digits=3)

# in both cases: power for indirect effects >= .849

messages.body_plain:
Ah, apologies. I was assuming you were using multiple groups.

I put an example with some made up data on https://rstudio.cloud/project/2385396 .

It's just like regression. Create 4 dummy coded groups, and omit a different one each time.

This code creates the groups:

wide_dat <- wide_dat %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    g1 = groups == 1,
    g2 = groups == 2,
    g3 = groups == 3,
    g4 = groups == 4,
  )

Then in your model you put either:
  i + s ~ g2 + g2 + g3 + g4

or
  i + s ~ g1 + g2 + g3

Then in the first model, each group is compared to group 1,

Regressions:
                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value
  i ~
    g2                0.010    0.076    0.130
    g3                0.082    0.076    1.083
    g4               -0.002    0.076   -0.027
  s ~
    g2                0.001    0.040    0.022
    g3               -0.026    0.040   -0.642
    g4                0.033    0.040    0.833

And in the second model, each is compared to group 4.
Regressions:
                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value
  i ~
    g1                0.002    0.076    0.027
    g2                0.012    0.076    0.157
    g3                0.084    0.076    1.110
  s ~
    g1               -0.033    0.040   -0.833
    g2               -0.032    0.040   -0.811
    g3               -0.059    0.040   -1.475

So in the first model, which compares everything to group 1 the slopes for g4 are -0.002 and 0.033. The second model, which compares everything to g4, the slopes for g1 are 0.002 and -0.033. We just reverse the sign.

(And you can do it again for the other two groups).

Jeremy

messages.body_plain:
Ecenaz,
The thing that stands out to me is that the other indicators on F3 have extremely small loadings.  This seems to suggest that R13 is not related to the other indicators on that factor.  I would try fixing the R13 loading to zero to see what happens to F3 when it reflects only common variance between the other indicators exclusive of R13.  I would also look at the correlation residuals to see what correlations between the indicators are not being fit well.  It could be that R13 is associated with one or more indicators on another factor in a way that is not accounted for by the general factor.  You may have to either remove R13 from the model or free some unique variance covariances.  It can be helpful to compare the correlation residuals to the correlations side by side (or in each triangle of a square matrix).  My guess is that the F13 loading estimate reflects misspecification somewhere else in the model.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

Dear Brett,
thank you very much for your response and your pointers to the literature. We will definitively have a look.

Nevertheless, it would be great to get some feedback on our analysis. Thus, with the hope to get some more insights, here's the reproducible example:
https://osf.io/shuxk/

Looking forward to your responses

Brett schrieb am Freitag, 8. Juli 2022 um 01:58:24 UTC+2:
> Please provide a minimal reproducible example for assistance with errors and discrepancies (see  https://stackoverflow.com/help/minimal-reproducible-example)
>
> It appears that "ordered" models the endogenous variables with the probit link based on the cumulative normal rather than the logit based on the cumulative logistic. These may differ at times, although usually modestly. Numerical error also can produce slightly different results if tolerances, starting values, etc. differ. See https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/mG5Mjrf2jgo/m/YGC-kR9oDAAJ
>
> If you need help understanding SEM more generally - interpretation, covariance structures, assumptions, dealing with non-normality, etc. - I'd recommend picking up a SEM text like Bollen (1989) and eventually visiting the SEMNet archives. If you want to know in more detail what the black box of the software is doing, you'll want to review this group and read the lavaan paper(s).
>
>
> On Thu, Jul 7, 2022, 3:44 AM 'Thomas Kettig' via lavaan <lav...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> > Hello all –
> >
> > I'm also on Fabian's team for this project, and we'd be appreciative of any help in figuring out why we see this discrepancy in our results! We'd be happy to supply more information about why we're trying to use SEM for our research questions, and can share some data if it helps better understand how lavaan works.
> >
> > Thomas
> >
> > On Friday, 1 July 2022 at 09:53:35 UTC+1 fabian.t...@googlemail.com wrote:
> > > Dear All,
> > > me and my colleagues are new to the SEM world and are struggling to reconcile the ANOVA and SEM results. We hope, you can help us explaining what is going on in our analysis by answering a couple of our questions. (I am sorry right away if I do not use the terminology correctly).
> > >
> > > ###########################################################
> > > Let me give you some background. We are trying to predict a binomial endogenous variable  (our dependent variable) by means of a set of categorical exogenous variables (our predictors) that all have two levels. But I'd like to focus only on one of those combinations.
> > > Our levels are basically zeros and ones. The table below shows you the distribution of our data:
> > >
> > >      endo
> > > exo    0   1
> > >  0 993   9
> > >  1 960  99
> > >
> > > The typical approach in my community would be to fit a glm, that transforms the data into logits. When I fit a glm with this data in the for like this:
> > > mod <- glm(pre~br)
> > >
> > > I get the following results:
> > >
> > >
> > >          Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
> > > (Intercept)  -4.0662     0.3361 -12.098  < 2e-16 ***
> > > endo = 1            1.1555     0.4105   2.815  0.00487 **
> > >
> > >
> > > informing me that the difference between 0 and 1 is logit = 1.155.
> > >
> > > We found that when one uses binomial variables, SEM can be informed about this by setting "ordered = TRUE".  When I run the following model:
> > >
> > > mod1 <-lavaan::sem('pre ~ br', data=DF, ordered = TRUE)
> > >
> > > I get the following summary:
> > >
> > > Regressions:
> > >                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
> > >   endo ~
> > >    exo                1.047    0.134    7.809    0.000
> > >
> > >
> > > telling me that the effect of the exogenous variable is significant. However, what does the estimate mean? What does the estimate represent? How is this value calculated and why does it differ from the glm?
> > >
> > >
> > > #################################################
> > > Another question that arose is that when I fit another relation, I get the following warning message:
> > >
> > >   The variance-covariance matrix of the estimated paramet
> > > ers (vcov)
> > >    does not appear to be positive definite! The smallest e
> > > igenvalue
> > >    (= 5.421011e-20) is close to zero. This may be a sympto
> > > m that the
> > >    model is not identified.
> > >
> > > I understand that the model failed to converge, but I wonder why, given that the glm fitted the data without problems:
> > >
> > > Coefficients:
> > >            Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
> > > (Intercept)   -20.57     819.59  -0.025    0.980
> > > endo = 1             18.53     819.59   0.023    0.982
> > >
> > > The failure to converge is even more surprising given that when I set "ordered = FALSE", it runs smoothly and provides me with a result.
> > >
> > >
> > > ################################################################
> > >
> > > Another aspect concerns level of significance.
> > > When I fit the exogenous only with one endogenous variable, then SEM informs me that there is no significant effect. However, when I include multiple endogenous variables, it turns out to be significant. Is this because SEMs suffer from something like collinearity that may cause enhancement?
> > >
> > > Thank you very much for your help.
> > >
> > >
> > >

> https://osf.io/shuxk/

That helps.

First, when ordered = TRUE, lavaan uses the *probit* link. Using glm(),
can you switch to the probit link as follows:

mod1 <- glm(endo~exo1, data = DF1[DF1$exo2 == 'final',], family =
binomial(link = "probit"))

and the regression coefficient (0.4943) will match that of lavaan.

About the warning: in the 'medial' subset, you have:

 > tmp <- DF1[DF1$exo2 == 'medial',]
 > table(tmp$endo, tmp$exo1)

       0   1
   0 468 611
   1   0  80

and this will cause trouble as the (estimated) threshold for endo will
be extremely large. Glm does not suffer from this (usually), but lavaan
uses a more complicated estimation procedure.

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
If you did not get an error message about statistical identification, this looks like a model that at least "nearly not identified." With only one indicator having a substantial loading, the model for factor f3 would fail identification tests if this were a conventional model. I'm not sure you can salvage this model without better indicators for f3.

Daniel's suggestion of nonconvergence is also a possibility. To overcome that problem, you might try setting plausible starting values for loadings on f3 in particular--probably values around 0.3 for all of those loadings and values of 0.10 for those observed variables' residual variances.

On Sun, Jul 24, 2022 at 9:40 AM 'Nickname' via lavaan <lav...@googlegroups.com> wrote:

> Ecenaz,
> The thing that stands out to me is that the other indicators on F3 have extremely small loadings.  This seems to suggest that R13 is not related to the other indicators on that factor.  I would try fixing the R13 loading to zero to see what happens to F3 when it reflects only common variance between the other indicators exclusive of R13.  I would also look at the correlation residuals to see what correlations between the indicators are not being fit well.  It could be that R13 is associated with one or more indicators on another factor in a way that is not accounted for by the general factor.  You may have to either remove R13 from the model or free some unique variance covariances.  It can be helpful to compare the correlation residuals to the correlations side by side (or in each triangle of a square matrix).  My guess is that the F13 loading estimate reflects misspecification somewhere else in the model.

messages.subject: Re: Is there any solution to improve factor loading?
messages.subject_clean: Is there any solution to improve factor loading?
messages.body_plain:
What do you mean by "too low?" There is no such thing as "improving" factor loadings - they are one of the infinite solutions to the factor analytic problem.

If your concern is that some items have low loadings when you think they should have high loadings (relative to others), you may have misspecified the factor structure - in essence, your latent factor isn't measuring what you expect it to capture. Alternatively, you have non-classically noisy items or are mistaken about their importance.

In any case, it is fine to have items with low loadings and in some cases dropping them can change the substantive interpretation of your factor(s). That being said, extremely low loadings (e.g. standardized 0.01) almost always suggest some sort of error or misunderstanding.

messages.subject: Re: Why CFA Excluding Cases and How to Override?
messages.subject_clean: Why CFA Excluding Cases and How to Override?
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

This is because the default in lavaan is to perform listwise deletion. You can add the argument "missing = fiml" to your cfa command and it will handle the missing values using Full Information Maximum Likelihood, which is not imputation. I would also use Maximum-Likelihood with robust standard-errors with the argument "estimator = MLR" to account for any non-normality in your data (The default is ML). Here are the resources for both issues:

Enders, C. K., & Bandalos, D. L. (2001). The relative performance of full information maximum likelihood estimation for missing data in structural equation models. Structural equation modeling, 8(3), 430-457.
Zhong, X., & Yuan, K. H. (2011). Bias and efficiency in structural equation modeling: Maximum likelihood versus robust methods. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 46(2), 229-265.

Hope this helps,

Alejandro

messages.subject_clean: Lavaan SEM and SPSS regression results are different
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Sorry for the confusion.
We ran the regressions in SPSS as our preliminary step of our research. We wanted to see how the IVs related with the DVs, so we simply ran several regressions in SPSS to do so.
We later decided to focus on SEM to conduct our research, and the model fit quite well after some modifications (CFI: 0.938, TLI: 0.928, RMSEA:  0.050, SRMR:  0.041).
However the regressions in SEM turned out to be contradictory to the regression results in SPSS we ran earlier.

By "I use the mean of the factor to do the regression analysis in SPSS" I mean I simply compute the mean of factor by adding all the items and divide it by the number of items. For example, FD_mean = (FD_1+FD_2+FD_3)/3. And we use these factor means as our IVs and DVs to run the regressions in the preliminary step.

We're surprised how regression coefficients can be this different in these two cases.

Thanks again for the response.
Please let me know if I did not make myself clear.

messages.subject: Re: Lavaan SEM and SPSS regression results are different
messages.subject_clean: Lavaan SEM and SPSS regression results are different
messages.body_plain:
i suspect what you mean is that either the values of the paths or the signs of the paths changed when you moved to SEM.
this can happen for at least 2 reasons.
1. SEM includes residuals which are retained in the predictors in regression.
2. SEM isolates the unique effect of correlated or multicollinear predictors. if the correlation between predictors is weak then it is possible to have a non-transitive impact on a dependent variable. So if A+B are positively correlated, you expect their effect on C to be equally possible. But SEM can identify the unique effect of A and B on C which can be A+B positive, but A+C positive and B+C negative. transitivity of relations is not required when A+B has a correlation much lower than 1.00

I would try running exactly the same regression in Lavaan and SPSS, with the same data (i.e. a saturated model, something like:

PU ~ capabiity_mean + FD_mean +  CM_mean  + AT_mean

)

That should give identical estimates, standard errors, etc (to 3rd decimal place or so).

If you've established that that is the same, then you can start to explore the differences.

But we'd expect SEM to give different results - if it gave the same results as regression it wouldn't have a purpose. (Also, check your standardized parameters.)

messages.subject: Re: Why CFA Excluding Cases and How to Override?
messages.subject_clean: Why CFA Excluding Cases and How to Override?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jonathan,

you can simply report the missingness in your variables for this. This can be done in different ways. For example, if the CFA is central to your analysis,  you could add a "%NA" column to the table where you present item details (e.g., loadings, wording). If the CFA is less central or you don't present such a table, you could describe the Nmin = and Nmax =, the minimum and maximum number of observations used for the analysis, in the text or in the table including the fit indices of the CFA. In any case, the missings for your items can be computed easily with base R functions such as table(data$your_item, NA = "always") for single items, colSums(is.na <http://is.na>(data)) for the whole DB, or using special packages such as this one <https://rdrr.io/cran/questionr/man/freq.na.html>. This resource explains in detail best practices to discuss missingness in your manuscript:

Newman, D. A. (2014). Missing data: Five practical guidelines. Organizational Research Methods, 17(4), 372-411.

Hope this helps,

Alejandro

messages.subject_clean: Issues with summary output on Jupyter Notebook since update
messages.body_plain:
First some background:

In >= 0.6-12, the summary() function is completely silent (following
'standard' R protocols). This means that

out <- summary(fit, fit.measures = TRUE)

should not print anything to the screen any longer. Instead, a list with
ingredients is stored in 'out'. You can then 'print' the content of out
by just typing

out

What 'should' happen is that R finds the corresponding printing
function, which is

lavaan:::print.lavaan.summary(out)

This should all happen automatically when you just type

summary(fit, fit.measures = TRUE)

I have no experience with Jupyter Notebooks. In anycase, reboot first.
If you type

out <- summary(fit, fit.measures = TRUE)

what is the output of

class(out)?

It should be "lavaan.summary" "list". Do you get any output if you use

lavaan:::print.lavaan.summary(out)?

lavaan is just using R's standard S3 system to dispatch the print()
function to print.lavaan.summary(). Is Jupyter Notebook somehow
interfering with this print() function?

Yves.

messages.subject: RE: Lavaan SEM and SPSS regression results are different
messages.subject_clean: Lavaan SEM and SPSS regression results are different
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

from my point of view we have not received enough information from Hazel. There can be many reasons for these results (some have already been addressed). In the simplest case, one or another indicator was reverse coded and that was not taken into account when calculating the means.

Example:

library(lavaan)

pop.model <- "
f1 =~ 1.0 * v1 + 0.8 * v2 + 0.9 * v3
f2 =~ 1.0 * v4 + -1.0 * v5 + -0.9 * v6
f2 ~ 0.6 * f1
"

model <- "
f1 =~ v1 + v2 + v3
f2 =~ v4 + v5 + v6
f2 ~ f1
"

set.seed(1)
data <- simulateData(pop.model, sample.nobs = 100000)
fit <- sem(model = model, data = data)
pe <- parameterEstimates(fit)
pe[pe$op == "~",]

data$f1 <- (data$v1 + data$v2 + data$v3) / 3
data$f2 <- (data$v4 + data$v5 + data$v6) / 3

summary(lm(f2 ~ f1, data = data))

Best

Christian

On Fri, Jul 29, 2022 at 1:12 AM Yves Rosseel <yros...@gmail.com> wrote:

> First some background:
>
> In >= 0.6-12, the summary() function is completely silent (following
> 'standard' R protocols). This means that
>
> out <- summary(fit, fit.measures = TRUE)
>
> should not print anything to the screen any longer. Instead, a list with
> ingredients is stored in 'out'. You can then 'print' the content of out
> by just typing
>
> out
>
> What 'should' happen is that R finds the corresponding printing
> function, which is
>
> lavaan:::print.lavaan.summary(out)
>
> This should all happen automatically when you just type
>
> summary(fit, fit.measures = TRUE)
>
>
> I have no experience with Jupyter Notebooks. In anycase, reboot first.
> If you type
>
> out <- summary(fit, fit.measures = TRUE)
>
> what is the output of
>
> class(out)?
>
> It should be "lavaan.summary" "list". Do you get any output if you use
>
> lavaan:::print.lavaan.summary(out)?
>
> lavaan is just using R's standard S3 system to dispatch the print()
> function to print.lavaan.summary(). Is Jupyter Notebook somehow
> interfering with this print() function?
>
> Yves.
